title: Letter and Typewriter
premise: In the winter of 1919, Silas Underhill, a battlefield nurse who spent twelve years recording in a hidden ledger the names and deaths that officers erased from official reports, is trapped when the seasonal bridge over the river closes, stranding her in the garrison town of Marrow's Ford alongside the very commanders whose omissions she documented. As a victors' historical commission arrives to write the official record before spring, Silas must decide whether to stay silent — as she always has — or place her ledger on the record, knowing it will implicate the man who once saved her life and endanger the soldiers who trusted her with their truths. When her ledger is stolen and one witness is killed, she races through the frozen weeks to reconstruct testimony from living mouths before the ice breaks and the commission departs. In the end she testifies at cost to her own safety and reputation, trading her invisibility for the names of the dead, and leaves across the broken ice carrying only a typewriter and a copy of every page.
about_author: Beatrix Ishikawa is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military correspondence and became obsessed with the letters that never made it into official histories. She writes from a farmhouse full of typewriters, none of which agree with each other.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Establishing her double life: by day the unremarkable nurse who mends what officers break, by night the keeper of 214 names the reports omit. The bridge closes for the season with her still on the wrong side of the river. Beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Small Silences
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter tracing how Silas learned which silences keep people safe, from her first field hospital to the massacre at Kessel Ravine she alone recorded fully. Her mentor's warning: 'A ledger is a confession you haven't been caught making.' Beat: guilt sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Commission Arrives
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Three historians of the victorious alliance reach Marrow's Ford to fix the official record before spring; among them is Edmund Hale, the officer whose life Silas saved and whose signature sits on the report that erases Kessel Ravine. Beat: the past walking through the door.

chapters.title: Tea with the Man I Saved
chapters.summary: Silas and Edmund meet again after six years; he is warm, grateful, and utterly certain his version of events is mercy rather than lie. She says nothing about the ledger but cannot sleep. Beat: loyalty and truth pulling in opposite directions for the first time on the page.

chapters.title: What Private Okafor Told Me
chapters.summary: Silas visits Tomas Okafor, a wounded veteran of the ravine now dying slowly in the town's charity ward, who begs her to make his account count for something. She begins collecting sworn statements. Beat: purpose kindling into danger.

chapters.title: The Typewriter in the Window
chapters.summary: Silas buys a battered typewriter from a pawnbroker to produce clean copies of testimony, hiding it behind curtains. The act of typing makes the ledger real in a way ink never did. Beat: quiet exhilaration before the fall.

chapters.title: Colonel Vane's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Edmund's superior, Colonel Vane, pays Silas an unsettlingly polite visit, praising her service and hinting that nurses who remember too much are reassigned to places with no bridges at all. Beat: threat wrapped in kindness.

chapters.title: The Stolen Pages
chapters.summary: Silas returns to find her room searched and half the ledger gone — taken with a precision that means someone close told them where to look. Suspicion falls on everyone she has trusted. Beat: betrayal and paranoia.

chapters.title: Okafor Stops Breathing
chapters.summary: Tomas Okafor dies the night before he was to sign his statement; the ward doctor calls it his wounds, but Silas sees the timing for what it is. Grief hardens into open war. Beat: the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: The Widow's Testimony
chapters.summary: Silas's POV interwoven with Marta Okafor's. His widow, who has spent years pretending not to know anything, chooses to speak, giving Silas letters Tomas mailed home that corroborate the ravine account. Beat: courage inherited from the dead.

chapters.title: Edmund Reads the Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas confronts Edmund with her surviving pages. He reads all night and admits he signed the false report believing silence would protect the survivors' pensions — protection built on erasure. Beat: loyalty vs. truth embodied in one man.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Vane offers Silas a formal commendation, a pension, and safe passage if she surrenders the ledger and testifies that the official record stands. She asks for one night to consider. Beat: temptation rendered almost reasonable.

chapters.title: The Night of Copies
chapters.summary: Silas types through the dark with Marta and the pawnbroker's daughter keeping watch, producing three copies of everything: one to hide, one to mail, one to carry. The typewriter's rhythm becomes a heartbeat. Beat: defiance as ritual.

chapters.title: The Informant
chapters.summary: Silas discovers the informant was the young ward clerk she trained herself — a boy who traded the pages for his brother's release from a penal unit. She cannot hate him and refuses to let him disappear from her own record. Beat: mercy as a discipline.

chapters.title: Ice Groaning on the River
chapters.summary: The thaw begins early; the commission prepares to leave within days, and Vane moves to have Silas committed to a rest facility on grounds of 'war hysteria.' Time collapses. Beat: rising panic under a calm surface.

chapters.title: What the Dead Would Sign
chapters.summary: Silas walks the ravine itself, now a picnic ground, gathering final corroboration from a farmer who buried the unnamed dead and kept their tags. She adds the farmer's name to her own ledger of witnesses. Beat: communion with the dead.

chapters.title: The Hearing That Wasn't One
chapters.summary: Silas forces the issue by requesting to give evidence to the commission formally; Vane arranges instead a closed session meant to discredit her. She enters expecting ambush. Beat: the trap closing.

chapters.title: Two Hundred Fourteen Names
chapters.summary: Climax. Before the commission, Silas reads every name aloud from memory while Marta lays the letters and tags on the table; Edmund, breaking with Vane, confirms the falsified report under oath. The room's silence finally belongs to the dead. Beat: catharsis through testimony.

chapters.title: The Price Named Aloud
chapters.summary: Aftermath of the hearing: Vane is relieved of the commission but escapes punishment; Silas loses her post, her references, and her anonymity. Edmund offers her escape and more; she declines both. Beat: victory that costs everything it should.

chapters.title: The Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: The river cracks open overnight. Silas mails one copy of the record to a newspaper editor in the capital, hides the second beneath the chapel floor where Okafor worshipped, and packs the third with her typewriter. Beat: release after long compression.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: Silas crosses the reopened bridge at dawn, past Vane's cold salute and the clerk's ashamed one, carrying nothing visible but a typewriter case. For the first time in twelve years she is entirely visible and entirely herself. Beat: quiet triumph.

chapters.title: Letter and Typewriter
chapters.summary: Epilogue, 1921. From a rented room in another country, Silas types the first page of a book titled with the number 214, enclosing a letter to each family she can find. The last line: some silences keep people safe; the rest just keep the dead waiting. Beat: inheritance passed on.
